models.collectorNote: Unmodified STIs — especially 2004–2007 US cars and clean GC-era imports — are the appreciating ones. A modified WRX is worth what the parts are worth, minus the worry.

generations.name: First generation WRX/STI
generations.note: Born from rally homologation: turbo flat-four, all-wheel drive, and Colin McRae sideways on every TV in Britain. Japanese STI versions were officially rated at 276 hp.

generations.name: Second generation ('Bugeye' and successors)
generations.note: America finally got the WRX in 2002 with 227 hp, then the STI in 2004 with 300 hp and a driver-controlled centre differential. The rivalry with Mitsubishi's Evo defined a decade.

generations.name: Current WRX
generations.note: A standalone model now, not an Impreza trim. The 2.4L turbo makes 271 hp, the plastic arch cladding divides opinion, and there is no STI — Subaru says the next one, if it comes, will be electrified.

models.intro: Rally car for the road, in continuous production in spirit since 1992. Turbo flat-four, all-wheel drive, and a bonnet scoop you could set your watch by. The STI versions are modern classics; the plain WRX is just a great all-weather fast car.
models.name: Impreza WRX

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: A Legacy wagon with raised suspension, cladding, and Paul Hogan in the ads. It invented a segment Australia and America both claim as their own idea.

generations.name: Fifth generation
generations.note: The wagon formula fully matured: quiet, spacious, and available with the 3.6L flat-six. The last Outback that still looked like a wagon first and an SUV second.

generations.name: Sixth generation
generations.note: Turbo power returned in XT models, and the Wilderness trim added lift, skid plates, and the confidence to actually use them. This is the template every 'rugged wagon' rival copies.

models.intro: The wagon that out-SUV'd the SUVs. Subaru jacked up a Legacy, added cladding, and accidentally created the blueprint for half the cars on American roads today — while never giving up the wagon part.
models.name: Outback

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Co-developed with Toyota (sold as the GT86/Scion FR-S) around one idea: low weight, low centre of gravity, rear drive, and just 200 hp — enough, if you drive it properly.

generations.name: Second generation
generations.note: The fix-everything sequel: a 2.4L engine with real mid-range torque, a stiffer shell, and the same manual gearbox. Widely considered one of the best affordable sports cars ever made.

models.intro: Proof a sports car doesn't need power, it needs balance. Subaru built the flat-four and the chassis; Toyota handled much of the rest. The result is the car driving instructors and racers agree on.
models.name: BRZ

generations.name: First generation
generations.note: Impreza bones, tall body, standard all-wheel drive — a formula nobody else was selling in 1997. The turbocharged Japanese-market cars hinted at what was coming.

generations.name: Second generation
generations.note: The XT is the sleeper of the 2000s: a WRX-adjacent turbo engine in a boxy family wagon. Manual XT cars are cult objects now, and increasingly hard to find unmodified.

generations.name: Fifth generation
generations.note: Bigger, safer, CVT-only, and turbo-free — the XT spirit moved to the Outback. As family transport, though, this is the most complete Forester ever sold.

models.intro: The tall, boxy, all-weather wagon-SUV that Vermont runs on. Early turbo XTs are cult cars; later ones are simply the sensible answer for snow-belt families who refuse to buy a crossover that looks like an egg.
models.name: Forester
